a: Happy is the person
p: Ashrei describes a good life to admire. It is not the same word as 'bless' (barukh).
b: The Psalter opens with ashrei, a word that points at someone and says: look how well off that person is. Older English Bibles say "Blessed is the man," which is fine, but it blurs a difference the Hebrew keeps: barukh, "blessed," is what God or people pronounce over someone; ashrei is a description of a happy, enviable life, common in wisdom writing (Proverbs 3:13; Proverbs 8:34). The word comes back at the end of Psalm 2 (2:12), so the two psalms are framed together. The Greek has makarios, the word of Jesus' beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–11). The Hebrew says "the man" (ha-ish), but the teaching is for anyone, as the plural "righteous" of 1:5–6 shows.

a: does not walk by the advice of the wicked
p: Three verbs, three places, three kinds of people: a picture of sliding into evil, or of a whole life kept clear of it.
b: The verse moves from walking to standing to sitting, and from the wicked (resha'im) to sinners to mockers. Many readers, from the rabbis to modern preachers, see a downward slide: first you take advice from bad people, then you linger on their road, then you settle among those who scoff at God. Others think the three lines simply cover all of life, moving and resting, as Deuteronomy 6:7 does ("when you are sitting in your house and when you are out on the road, when you go to bed"). The "mockers" (letsim) are the cynics of Proverbs, who laugh at correction (Proverbs 9:7–8; Proverbs 21:24).

a: the law of the LORD
p: Torah means instruction. Here it is God's whole teaching, which the Psalter itself now offers to the reader.
b: Torah is rendered "law" on this site, but its root sense is "instruction, teaching," the guidance a parent gives a child (Proverbs 1:8). In Psalm 1 it is more than a list of commands: it is God's revealed will, delightful and life-giving (compare 19:7–11; 119). Many scholars think the editors put Psalm 1 at the front to turn the whole collection into a book of torah to be studied, and the five-book division of the Psalter may echo the five books of Moses (Midrash Tehillim on 1:1 says, "Moses gave Israel the five books of the Torah, and David gave Israel the five books of Psalms"). Christians have read the verse of Christ, who delights in the Father's will (40:8).

a: the LORD
t: The LORD and the name YHWH
p: Small capitals stand for God's own name, YHWH. 'Lord' in ordinary type is a title.
b: Where the Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, God's personal name, the Plain follows most English Bibles and prints "the LORD" in capitals, because Jewish readers say Adonai, "my Lord," in its place out of reverence. "Lord" in ordinary type (2:4; 8:1) translates Adonai, a title. Elohim is "God." In the Psalms the choice of name is not random: Book I (1–41) uses YHWH far more often than Elohim, while most of 42–83 prefer Elohim, which is why Psalm 14 and its twin Psalm 53 differ in their name for God (see 14:2).

a: he murmurs over his law
p: Hagah is a sound: the low voice of someone reading aloud, or a dove's moan. Ancient reading was spoken.
b: The verb hagah is often translated "meditate," which suggests silent thinking. But hagah is a sound word: a lion growls over its prey with it (Isaiah 31:4), a dove moans (Isaiah 38:14), a tongue speaks (35:28). Ancient people usually read aloud, under their breath, and memorized by repeating. The picture is of someone muttering the words of God's teaching over and over, day and night, as Joshua is told to do (Joshua 1:8). The same verb returns at 2:1, where the nations "murmur" their empty plans: two kinds of murmuring, one over God's teaching and one against God's king.

a: like a tree set out by channels of water
p: Not a wild tree but a transplanted one, set beside irrigation channels. Jeremiah 17:5–8 uses the same image.
b: Shatul means "transplanted," set out on purpose by a gardener; palgei mayim are channels cut for irrigation, as in the gardens of Mesopotamia and Egypt. The righteous do not grow by chance: they have been planted where the water is. Jeremiah 17:5–8 uses almost the same picture for the one who trusts in the LORD, set against the desert shrub of the one who trusts in people. The image grows into the temple trees of 52:8 and 92:12–14, the river of Ezekiel 47:12 and the tree of life beside the river in Revelation 22:2.

a: they are like the husks the wind drives off
p: At harvest, farmers tossed grain into the wind. The heavy kernels fell; the light husks blew away.
b: On the threshing floor, usually a flat rock on a windy hilltop, farmers loosened the husks from the grain and then threw the mixture into the air with a wooden fork. The wind carried off the chaff, the light, dry husks, and the heavy grain fell back to be gathered. The wicked, for all their noise, have no weight. The image is common in the prophets and in John the Baptist's preaching (Isaiah 17:13; Hosea 13:3; Matthew 3:12). The Greek adds "from the face of the earth" and repeats "not so" ("Not so the wicked, not so").

a: the wicked will not stand when judgment comes
p: A court case in this life, or the last judgment? Jewish and Christian readers have heard both.
b: "Stand" is a legal word: to stand in court is to win one's case (compare 130:3). Many scholars think of judgment within history, as when the city gate hears a case or the righteous gather for worship and the wicked have no place among them (15:1; 24:3–4). The Targum and many rabbis read it of the world to come: the wicked will not be acquitted on the day of great judgment. The Greek "will not rise up in judgment" (ouk anastesontai) was read by some church fathers as a statement about resurrection, though most took it to mean the wicked would not be vindicated. The parallel line, "in the company of the righteous," points to a community from which they are excluded.

a: the LORD knows the road of the righteous
t: To know is to care for
p: In Hebrew, God's 'knowing' is personal: he watches over, cares for and chooses.
b: Yada', "know," in the Bible often means far more than awareness. God "knew" Abraham, that is, chose him (Genesis 18:19); he "knew" Israel in the desert (Hosea 13:5); Jesus will tell some, "I never knew you" (Matthew 7:23). So the line means the LORD watches over, cares for and stands by the way of the righteous. The wicked's road has no such keeper, and so it is "lost" (to'ved), the same word as in 2:12: "you will be lost on your road." Psalm 1 ends with that word, and Psalm 2 ends with it too, a sign that the two were meant to be read together.

a: Why do the nations gather in an uproar
p: The apostles prayed Psalm 2:1–2 after Peter and John were threatened (Acts 4:25–28).
b: In Acts 4:24–28, the believers in Jerusalem quote 2:1–2 as words of "our father David" spoken by the Holy Spirit, and apply them to Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, who gathered against Jesus, God's anointed. That is one of the earliest Christian readings of a psalm. The Hebrew verb ragash means to be in commotion, to throng noisily; the Greek has ephryaxan, "snorted, raged"; older English Bibles say "rage" (the KJV), and the Latin has fremuerunt, "roared". Psalm 2 has no title in the Hebrew; Acts names David as its author, following the tradition of its time.

a: the peoples murmur over empty plans
p: The nations 'murmur' (hagah) just as the righteous person 'murmurs' over God's law.
b: The verb is hagah again (see 1:2). The happy person murmurs over the LORD's teaching day and night; the peoples murmur their plots against the LORD. The word-play is one of several links that bind Psalms 1 and 2 into a double introduction to the Psalter. The plans are riq, "empty, for nothing": they will come to nothing, as 2:4 shows.

a: against the LORD and against his anointed one
p: The king of Israel was anointed with oil. 'Messiah' and 'Christ' both come from this word.
b: Meshicho, "his anointed one," is the word from which "Messiah" comes; its Greek translation christos gives "Christ." In ancient Israel, oil was poured on a king's head when he was made king (1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Samuel 16:13), and the king was called "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:6). In its first setting Psalm 2 speaks of the king of David's line in Jerusalem. After the exile, when there was no king, Jews and later Christians read it of a coming king. The Psalms of Solomon 17:21–32, from the first century BC, already echo Psalm 2 in describing a coming son of David.

a: Let us tear off their straps
p: The rebels picture the LORD's rule as a yoke on an ox, held on with leather straps and ropes.
b: Moserot are the leather bands that tied a yoke onto an ox's neck (Jeremiah 27:2). Vassal kings who paid tribute to an empire spoke of its "yoke," and rebellion was "breaking the yoke" (Jeremiah 2:20; Jeremiah 28:10–11). Here the subject nations of the Davidic king plot to break free, which may reflect the moment a new king came to the throne, when vassals often tested a young ruler. The psalm's answer is that the yoke is the LORD's own.

a: Seated in the heavens, he laughs.
p: A bold picture. It is not cruelty, but the scale of the contest: rebels against heaven are absurd.
b: The kings of the earth stand; the LORD sits, enthroned. The kings plot; he laughs. The same laughter returns in 37:13 and 59:8. Readers have found the picture troubling, but its point is the difference in power: the uprising of the nations is no real threat. Jewish interpreters noted that this laughter belongs to the moment of judgment, not to God's attitude toward suffering. Augustine took it to mean that God's wisdom sees the end of the plot from the beginning, and that the laughter is given to his people, who can see their enemies' plans already overturned.

a: I myself have put my king in place
p: The verb nasakh may mean 'install' or 'pour out', as oil is poured in anointing. The Greek makes the king speak.
b: Nasakhti is usually taken from nasakh, "to pour out" (a drink offering), here "to install" by anointing; some link it with a root meaning "to weave, form" (compare 139:13, "you wove me"). The Old Greek reads the verse differently: "But I was set up as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain," so that the king, not the LORD, speaks, and goes straight on into 2:7. The Hebrew, with the LORD speaking, is followed here. Zion was the ridge of Jerusalem where David put the ark (2 Samuel 6:12–17), and later the name of the temple mountain.

a: You are my son.
p: The king becomes God's son on the day he is crowned. The New Testament hears it at Jesus' baptism, resurrection and exaltation.
b: The words belong to the covenant with David: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14; compare Psalm 89:26–27). Ancient Near Eastern kings were often called sons of a god; in Israel the phrase is adoption language, spoken "this day," the day of coronation. The New Testament takes it up often. The voice at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration echoes it (Mark 1:11; Mark 9:7). Paul in Acts 13:33 applies "this day I have fathered you" to the resurrection; Hebrews 1:5 and Hebrews 5:5 to the Son's exaltation above the angels. Later Christian teaching on the eternal generation of the Son drew on the verse; Jewish interpreters (Rashi, Radak) read it of David or of the Messiah as God's chosen king, not as a divine son by nature.
r: 2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 89:26–27; Mark 1:11; Mark 9:7; Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5

a: This day I have fathered you.
p: The Hebrew yelidtikha is the verb for begetting. The king is adopted; the word is a family word.
b: Yelidtikha is "I have begotten you," the ordinary verb for a father having a child. Some modern versions soften it to "I have become your father," to show it is adoption, not birth. The Plain keeps the strong verb, because the New Testament and the creeds lean on it, and lets the note explain: "this day," the day of crowning, shows the sense is royal adoption. The Greek has gegenneka se, which the Nicene Creed's "begotten of the Father" echoes.

a: the far ends of the earth
t: A king of Jerusalem ruling the world?
p: The promise is far bigger than any king of Judah's real power. That gap is why later readers looked ahead.
b: No king in Jerusalem ever ruled "the ends of the earth." David's small empire reached from Edom to Damascus at most. Critical scholars see court language of the kind Egyptian and Assyrian kings used, given to Judah's king as an ideal (compare 72:8–11). Traditional Jewish readers apply the full promise to the Messiah (Talmud, Sukkah 52a, quotes 2:7–8 of the Messiah son of David). Christians apply it to Christ and the spread of the gospel to the nations (Matthew 28:18–19; Revelation 11:15). All agree that the psalm says more than any one king in Judah could fulfill.

a: learn your lesson
p: The imperatives turn from God's speech to the kings themselves: the psalm becomes an appeal.
b: Hivvaseru means "accept correction, be disciplined," from the word for a father's training (musar, Proverbs 1:2–8). The kings are not only threatened; they are invited to wisdom (haskilu, "show good sense"). The same choice of two roads that Psalm 1 put before one person, Psalm 2 puts before the rulers of the world.

a: be glad with trembling
p: Joy and fear together sound odd in English. Some scholars rearrange 2:11–12 to read 'kiss his feet with trembling'.
b: Gilu bi-re'adah, "rejoice with trembling," puts together two things English keeps apart. It may mean the exultant shout of subjects at a coronation, joined with the awe due to the LORD; Paul's "work out your salvation with fear and trembling" (Philippians 2:12) has a similar mix. Because the lines are hard, some modern scholars move the words around so that 2:11b–12a read "with trembling kiss his feet" (see the variant at 2:12). The Plain keeps the Hebrew order.

a: for his anger is quick to catch fire
p: Kim'at can mean 'soon' or 'only a little': his anger flares fast, or even a little of it is enough.
b: Kim'at means "in a moment, soon" or "a little." The KJV took the second: "when his wrath is kindled but a little." Most modern versions take the first. Either way, the point is urgency: the kings must decide now. Whose anger? In the Hebrew it may be the son's or the LORD's; the Greek supplies "the Lord."

a: Happy are all who shelter in him.
p: 'Happy' opened Psalm 1. Here it closes Psalm 2, framing both as the Psalter's double gateway.
b: Ashrei (1:1) returns, and so does the "road" that is "lost" (1:6). Together Psalms 1 and 2 form the Psalter's introduction: the way of the LORD's teaching (Psalm 1) and the rule of the LORD's king (Psalm 2). An old Jewish tradition counts them as one psalm: in the Talmud, Rabbi Yohanan says "the psalm David especially loved" begins and ends with ashrei (Bavli Berakhot 9b–10a), and some manuscripts of Acts 13:33 call 2:7 a verse of "the first psalm." "Shelter" (chasah), seeking refuge, becomes one of the key words of Book I (5:11; 7:1; 11:1; 16:1; 17:7).

a: A psalm of David, when he ran away from his son Absalom.
p: Psalm 3 is the first with a heading. It ties the prayer to David's flight in 2 Samuel 15–17.
b: Most psalms from 3 to 41 have headings. In the Hebrew Bible the heading is counted as verse 1, so in Hebrew Bibles the verse numbers of most psalms run one higher than in English; this site, like English Bibles, calls the title verse 0. "Of David" (le-david) can mean "by David," "for David," "about David" or "belonging to the David collection." This title points to 2 Samuel 15–17, when David fled Jerusalem barefoot and weeping as Absalom took the throne, and Shimei cursed him (2 Samuel 16:5–8). The psalm itself never names Absalom. Traditional readers take the title as David's own note; most scholars think editors added it, matching the psalm's "many" enemies (3:1) and its mention of sleep to the night of David's flight (2 Samuel 17:1–16). See the topic on psalm titles.

a: A psalm of David
p: Mizmor, 'a psalm', is a song meant to be sung to an instrument. It appears only in psalm titles.
b: Mizmor comes from zamar, to make music, especially by plucking strings. It is used only in the headings of the Psalms (57 times) and was translated into Greek as psalmos, a song sung to plucked strings, which gave the book its English name. Other heading words are shir, "a song" (as in the Songs of Ascents), tehillah, "a praise" (145), tefillah, "a prayer" (17:0), and the obscure maskil, miktam and shiggaion (see 7:0 and 16:0).

a: Selah
p: Selah appears 71 times in the Psalms and three times in Habakkuk 3. No one knows for sure what it means.
b: The word selah is kept as it is. Its meaning was already lost in ancient times. The Greek translators wrote diapsalma, perhaps "an interlude on the strings." The Targum and Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew rendered it "forever" (semper), and the Jewish prayer book follows that sense in some places. Many modern scholars link it with salal, "lift up," and think it told singers or players to raise their voices or instruments, or marked a pause or a place for a refrain or bowing. It is not read aloud as part of the sense in most synagogues and churches. It often stands at a turning point, as here, after the enemies' taunt.
r: Habakkuk 3:3; Habakkuk 3:9; Habakkuk 3:13; Psalm 46:3; Psalm 46:7; Psalm 46:11

a: There is no rescue for him in God.
p: The enemies say God will not save him. The psalm ends, 'Rescue is the LORD's!'
b: Yeshu'ah, rescue, salvation, victory, comes from the same root as the names Joshua and Jesus. The enemies' taunt in 3:2 and the psalm's last line in 3:8 use the same word, so the psalm answers its enemies point by point. In Second Samuel the cursing Shimei shouts that the LORD has handed the kingdom to Absalom as punishment (2 Samuel 16:7–8): the taunt is that God has given up on David.
orig: אֵין יְשׁוּעָתָה לּוֹ בֵאלֹהִים (ein yeshu'atah lo ve'lohim)

a: you raise my head
p: A head bowed in shame or mourning is lifted by the one who restores honor.
b: David left Jerusalem with his head covered in mourning (2 Samuel 15:30). To "lift someone's head" is to restore him: Pharaoh "lifted the head" of his cupbearer when he released him (Genesis 40:13), and a Babylonian king lifted the head of the exiled King Jehoiachin (2 Kings 25:27). God himself is "my honor" (kevodi), the dignity the enemies have stripped away.

a: I lay down and fell asleep
p: Sleeping in danger is the psalm's center. Christians also heard Christ's death and resurrection in it.
b: Lying down to sleep with an army hunting you is itself an act of trust (compare 4:8). The Hebrew verbs are past: the psalmist has already slept and woken, and takes that as proof that the LORD holds him up. From Justin Martyr and Irenaeus on, many church fathers read the verse as Christ's words about his death and resurrection: "I lay down and slept; I rose up, for the Lord sustained me" (so the Greek). Jewish tradition used it of trust at night, and the bedtime prayers of the Jewish prayer book draw on such psalm verses. Many churches sing Psalm 3 at the start of the night office or of morning prayer.

a: You have hit all my enemies across the jaw
p: The verbs look past: 'you have struck'. Many read them as confident prayer: 'strike them!'
b: The Hebrew perfect tense (hikkita, shibbarta) usually describes completed action. Some take the line as remembering past rescues; others as the "perfect of confidence," speaking of what God will surely do as if it were already done; others (and some modern versions) as a wish. Striking an enemy's cheek is an insult as well as a blow (1 Kings 22:24; Micah 5:1), and breaking a beast's teeth makes it harmless (58:6): the enemies, pictured as wild animals, lose their bite.

a: Let your blessing rest on your people.
t: From one man to a people
p: A prayer for a single fugitive ends with blessing on the whole people.
b: The last line widens the prayer. For David in flight, "your people" would include the Israelites who had followed Absalom; his prayer for them fits the king who wept for his rebel son (2 Samuel 18:33). For later Israel, singing the psalm in worship, the line turned one man's prayer into the congregation's.

a: For the music director
p: Lamnatseach heads 55 psalms. Its meaning is debated; the Greek has 'for the end'.
b: Lamnatseach comes from natsach, which in Chronicles means to direct or lead the temple music (1 Chronicles 15:21; 1 Chronicles 23:4). So most take the phrase as "for the leader" or "for the choir director," perhaps marking psalms from a collection used by the temple musicians. The Greek translators wrote eis to telos, "for the end," reading the root as "forever, to completion." Many church fathers read that as a pointer to Christ, "the end of the law" (Romans 10:4), or to the end of time. The Targum has "for praise." On "stringed instruments" (neginot), see the topic on music.

a: God of my right
p: The God who stands for my right: the one who will judge my case in my favor.
b: Elohei tsidqi is literally "God of my righteousness." In the Psalms, tsedeq often means being in the right in a dispute. The psalmist, slandered (4:2), appeals to the God who knows he is in the right and will defend it. It is not a claim to be sinless.

a: In my tight place you made room for me.
p: Distress in Hebrew is 'narrowness'. Rescue is being given room.
b: Tsar, "distress," is literally a narrow, tight place, and hirchavta, "you made wide," is to give space. The picture runs through the Psalms: God sets the feet in a broad place (31:8) and answers the one who calls from a narrow place by giving room (118:5). The verb is past: the psalmist remembers being rescued before and asks again.

a: You men of standing
p: Bene ish may mean people of rank, not just 'people'. The psalmist may be speaking to powerful accusers.
b: Hebrew has two phrases for human beings: bene adam, "sons of Adam," and the rarer bene ish, used here. In 49:2 and 62:9 the two stand side by side as "low and high," which suggests bene ish means men of standing. The psalmist may be addressing influential people who have damaged his reputation, or (on another view) Israelites who have turned to other gods for rain and harvest, if "what is worthless" and "what is false" are idols (compare 4:7; Jeremiah 16:19).

a: Be shaken, but do not sin.
p: Paul quotes the Greek of this line in Ephesians 4:26. The Hebrew verb can mean tremble or rage.
b: Rigzu means to quiver, shake, be stirred, whether with fear or with anger. The Greek translated orgizesthe, "be angry," and Paul quotes that wording in Ephesians 4:26: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger." In the psalm the sense is probably "tremble (before God), and stop sinning": the accusers are told to lie awake, think, and fall silent. Paul's use of the Greek is fair to its sense: strong feeling need not turn into sin.

a: raise the light of your face above us
p: The line echoes the priests' blessing of Numbers 6:24–26, with its shining and lifted face of God.
b: "Lift up the light of your face" combines two lines of the priests' blessing: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" and "May the LORD lift up his face toward you" (Numbers 6:25–26). In the ancient Near East a king's shining face meant favor; a hidden face meant rejection (13:1). The "many" who ask "Who will show us anything good?" may be people in a drought looking for rain and harvest (4:7). The psalmist turns their question into a prayer.

a: because you alone, LORD, settle me in safety
p: Levadad may mean the LORD alone keeps him safe, or that he sleeps alone, in safety, like Israel in Deuteronomy 33:28.
b: Levadad means "in isolation, alone." Most versions apply it to God: "you alone, LORD." But the same pair of words, badad and betach, "alone" and "in safety," describes Israel in Deuteronomy 33:28 ("Israel has settled in safety; / Jacob's spring stands apart"), so some scholars read: "you, LORD, make me dwell apart, in safety." Both readings end the evening psalm in calm. Jews and Christians alike have used Psalm 4 as a night prayer: the Rule of Benedict sets it first among the psalms of Compline every night (with Psalms 91 and 134), and the Roman Liturgy of the Hours sings it at Night Prayer on Saturday evening.

a: For the flutes
p: El-hanechilot is found only here. Most take it as 'for flutes'; the Greek read 'for her who inherits'.
b: Nechilot appears nowhere else. Many link it with chalil, "flute, pipe" (1 Samuel 10:5; Isaiah 30:29), so "with flutes." The Greek translators read it as from nachalah, "inheritance" ("for her who inherits"), and Rashi records a tradition that it names a melody or instrument. The meaning is uncertain.

a: At daybreak I set out my plea for you
p: 'Arak is used of laying out a sacrifice on the altar and of setting out a legal case.
b: The verb 'arak has no object here. It is used for laying wood and pieces of a sacrifice on the altar (Leviticus 1:7–8; 1 Kings 18:33) and for setting out arguments in court (Job 23:4; Job 33:5). So the psalmist may be preparing a morning offering, or laying out his case before God, or both. Morning was the time of the daily burnt offering (Exodus 29:38–39) and, in Israel's courts, the time justice was given (2 Samuel 15:2; Jeremiah 21:12). Then he "keeps watch," like a watchman waiting for the answer (Habakkuk 2:1).

a: Evil may not live with you as a guest.
p: Yegurkha uses the word for a resident guest. Evil may not lodge in God's house; compare Psalm 15.
b: Gur means to stay as a ger, a resident guest under another's protection. The same question opens Psalm 15: "who is welcome as a guest in your tent?" (15:1). Evil cannot claim the protection of the LORD's house. That is why the psalmist, by contrast, enters only "by the greatness of your loyal love" (5:7).

a: You hate everyone who does wrong.
p: The psalm says God hates evildoers. Interpreters have weighed this against God's love for sinners.
b: The Psalms speak of God's hatred bluntly (11:5; Proverbs 6:16–19). The phrase po'ale aven, "doers of wrong," may point to those who use harmful words or curses against others, as Mowinckel argued, or simply to evildoers. Christian readers have often followed Augustine: God hates the sin and loves the sinner as his creature, and calls him to turn. Others note that the Hebrew "hate" includes rejection, refusing to accept someone into one's presence, which fits 5:4–5: evil is not welcome in the temple.

a: by the greatness of your loyal love
p: Hesed is the faithful love of someone bound to you. It is God's love kept, not earned.
b: Hesed is rendered "loyal love" throughout this site. It is the kindness of someone who is committed to you, loyalty that goes beyond what duty requires: the love of a covenant partner, a friend, a family member. The psalmist does not enter the temple because he is better than the wicked of 5:4–6 but because of the abundance of God's hesed. The word appears more often in the Psalms than in the rest of the Hebrew Bible together (about 127 of some 250 times).

a: Toward your holy temple I will bow
t: A temple in a psalm of David?
p: David never saw Solomon's temple. But the word hekhal was also used of the tent-shrine at Shiloh.
b: Hekhal, "palace, temple," usually means the temple Solomon built after David's death. Scholars who date the psalm late take this as a sign that it was written or adapted for the temple. Traditional readers note that hekhal is used of the sanctuary at Shiloh before there was a temple (1 Samuel 1:9; 1 Samuel 3:3), and that "house" and "temple" can mean the LORD's dwelling in general, even in heaven (11:4; 18:6). Bowing "toward" the temple became a Jewish custom of prayer (1 Kings 8:29–30; Daniel 6:10).
r: 1 Samuel 1:9; 1 Samuel 3:3; 1 Kings 8:29–30; Daniel 6:10; Psalm 11:4; Psalm 138:2

a: their throat is a grave left open
p: Paul quotes this line in his chain of verses showing that all are under sin (Romans 3:13).
b: Paul strings together verses from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10 and 36 and Isaiah 59 in Romans 3:10–18, to show that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin. From this verse he takes "their throat is an open grave; they deceive with their tongues" (the Greek wording). An open grave smells of death and is ready to swallow: the enemies' speech kills. Their tongues "make smooth," flatter (yachaliqun), like the slippery lips of 12:2.

a: Hold them guilty, God.
p: The psalm asks God to condemn and expel the deceivers. It is a prayer for justice, not a private act of revenge.
b: Book I has many prayers like this, sharper ones too (see Psalm 35). Here the psalmist asks God to declare the liars guilty and let their schemes trip them, the same "pit" principle as 7:15–16 and 9:15. He leaves the verdict to God and calls them rebels against God, not merely against himself. Christian readers have prayed such lines in several ways: as prayers against evil itself, as prayers for God's justice for the oppressed, or as words they hand over to God rather than act on (compare Romans 12:19). See the topic on the curse psalms.

a: like a great shield
p: Tsinnah is the big shield that covered the whole body, not the small round one.
b: Hebrew has two words for shield: magen, the small round buckler (3:3; 7:10), and tsinnah, the large body shield, often carried by a shield-bearer in front of a soldier (1 Samuel 17:7). God's favor covers the righteous on every side.

a: On the sheminith
p: Sheminith means 'the eighth'. It may name an eight-stringed instrument, a tuning, or a tune.
b: Ha-sheminit, "the eighth," appears here, in Psalm 12:0 and in 1 Chronicles 15:21, where Levites play lyres "on the sheminith." Proposals include an eight-stringed lyre, a lower register (an octave), or the eighth of a set of tunes. Some church fathers read "the eighth" as the eighth day, the day of resurrection or the age to come, and so read Psalm 6 as a prayer looking to the last judgment (Augustine, on Psalm 6).

a: not in your anger, please, do not rebuke me
p: Christian tradition counts Psalm 6 first of seven 'penitential psalms': 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143.
b: The psalm does not confess a particular sin, but its opening asks God to discipline without destroying (compare Jeremiah 10:24, "correct me, LORD, but with justice, not in your anger"). Cassiodorus in the 500s grouped 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143 as the seven penitential psalms, and they were prayed in Lent, at confession and for the dying through the Middle Ages and the Reformation; Luther's first printed book (1517) was a commentary on them. In the Ashkenazi Jewish rite Psalm 6 is said in the daily Tachanun ("supplication") prayers after the morning and afternoon services on many weekdays, while one rests one's head on one's arm.
r: Jeremiah 10:24; Psalm 38:1; Psalm 32; Psalm 51; Psalm 130; Hebrews 12:5–11

a: my bones are in terror
p: The same word, bahal, is used for bones (6:2), soul (6:3) and enemies (6:10).
b: Nivhalu means to be terrified, thrown into panic. The psalm uses it three times: the sufferer's bones are terrified (6:2), his soul is in deep terror (6:3), and at the end he prays that his enemies will be terrified instead (6:10). The bones stand for the whole body, worn by illness (compare 22:14; 32:3). Most scholars read Psalm 6 as the prayer of someone seriously ill, who fears death (6:5) and whose enemies take his sickness as a sign of God's judgment.

a: My soul
p: Nefesh is not a soul inside a body but the living self: throat, breath, life, the whole person.
b: The Hebrew nefesh is usually translated "soul," but it does not mean a spirit that can leave the body. It can mean the throat (69:1), appetite (107:9), life (6:4, "pull my life free"), or simply "me" (3:2, "about me," literally "about my nefesh"). "My soul is in terror" means "I am terrified through and through." The Plain uses "soul," "life" or "me" by context.

a: And you, LORD, how long?
p: The broken line is the cry of lament. The question returns in Psalm 13 four times.
b: The sentence breaks off: "and you, LORD, until when?" Calvin noted that the unfinished sentence shows the force of the pain. "How long" (ad-matai, ad-anah) is the key question of lament (13:1–2; 74:10; 79:5; 90:13), and it comes back in the cry of the martyrs in Revelation 6:10. The Hebrew written text (Ketiv) has the feminine form of "you" ('at); the reading tradition (Qere) has the usual masculine. It is a spelling matter, not a change of meaning.

a: For among the dead no one calls you to mind.
p: The psalmist argues that if he dies, God loses a worshiper. Is this the Old Testament's last word on death?
b: "Among the dead" is literally "in death" (ba-mavet). "Calls you to mind" (zikhrekha, "remembrance of you") means remembering God in worship, naming him in praise. Several psalms argue this way (30:9; 88:10–12; 115:17), as does Hezekiah's prayer (Isaiah 38:18): the dead in Sheol do not join the temple's praise. Many scholars see here an early stage of Israel's thought, before a clear hope of resurrection (Daniel 12:2). Jewish interpreters such as Radak read it as speaking of what the dead can no longer do for God in this world, not of their extinction. Christians differ on what it implies for the state of the dead; see the box on the chapter page.

a: I make my bed swim
p: The bed swims and the couch melts. The Hebrew piles up images of weeping on purpose.
b: "I make my bed swim" (asecheh) and "I melt my couch" (amseh) are bold exaggerations, the kind of poetry that tells the truth of grief by overstating it. The Plain keeps them rather than flattening them to "I cry all night."

a: Leave me, every one of you who does wrong!
p: At the last judgment Jesus says to those he never knew, 'Get away from me, you who do lawlessness' (Matthew 7:23).
b: The sudden turn from tears to command is one of the most striking changes in the Psalms. Many scholars think that between 6:7 and 6:8 the sufferer received an answer, perhaps a priest's word of assurance in the temple (compare 1 Samuel 1:17–18). Jesus takes up this line in Matthew 7:23 and Luke 13:27, so that the words the sufferer spoke to his enemies become the words of the judge. On the change of mood in laments, see the topic on lament.

a: A shiggaion of David
p: A rare word, also in Habakkuk 3:1. It may mean a wild, passionate song or a lament.
b: Shiggaion (plural in Habakkuk 3:1) has been linked with shagah, "to wander, reel" (so a wild or irregular song), or with an Akkadian word shegu, a lament. Its meaning is unknown. The Greek has simply "a psalm."

a: about the words of Cush, a Benjaminite
p: No Cush of Benjamin appears in Samuel. He may be a slanderer in Saul's court, or a code name.
b: Second Samuel mentions a Cushite messenger who brought news of Absalom's death (2 Samuel 18:21–32), but he was not from Saul's tribe of Benjamin. Saul's courtiers slandered David (1 Samuel 24:9; 1 Samuel 26:19), and Shimei the Benjaminite cursed him (2 Samuel 16:5–8). The Targum and the Talmud identify "Cush" with Saul himself, as a nickname (Bavli Moed Katan 16b), and Rashi follows. The psalm's oath of innocence (7:3–5), "if I have harmed the one at peace with me," fits the time David spared Saul's life (1 Samuel 24:10–11). The Greek reads "Chousi son of Iemeni," perhaps thinking of Hushai (2 Samuel 15:32).

a: if this is what I have done
p: The psalmist swears an oath and calls down a curse on himself if he is guilty. Ancient law used such oaths.
b: When there were no witnesses, Israelite law allowed an accused person to clear himself by an oath at the sanctuary (Exodus 22:8–11; 1 Kings 8:31–32). The oath took the form "If I have done X, may Y happen to me," as in Job 31. Psalm 7 has this shape: "if this is what I have done... then let the enemy chase me" (7:3–5). Many scholars think it was the prayer of a falsely accused person who came to the temple for God's verdict. "This" is not named: the title supplies a setting.

a: or stripped my enemy without cause
p: The verb chalats usually means 'rescue'. Here it seems to mean 'strip, plunder'. The KJV took it as rescue.
b: Va'achaltsah normally means "I rescued" (6:4). Read that way, the line is a parenthesis, as in the KJV: "yea, I have delivered him that without cause is mine enemy," a reminder that David spared Saul (1 Samuel 24). But the parallel with "done harm" suggests the other sense of the root, "pull off, strip" (as clothing is stripped in 2 Samuel 2:21), and most modern versions read "plundered." Both readings are possible.

a: Let the nations gather around you in assembly
t: A personal case before the world's judge
p: A private quarrel becomes a scene of world judgment.
b: The psalmist's case is small, a slander, but he asks the LORD to take his seat as judge of all peoples (7:7–8). The image is the divine court, where the nations gather (compare 82:1, 8). Some scholars think the psalm was used by the king, whose cause was Israel's cause; others see a private person who knows that the God who judges nations is the same God who hears him. The verb "take your place again" (shuvah, "return") may be read shevah, "sit (as judge)," with a small change of vowels.

a: as my right deserves
p: He is not claiming to be sinless. He claims to be innocent of this charge.
b: Requests to be judged "according to my righteousness and my integrity" (ke-tsidqi u-khetummi) can sound proud to Christian ears (compare 143:2). In context the psalmist means that he is in the right in this dispute. Calvin made the same point: David does not boast of his whole life but of a good conscience in this case. The word tom, "integrity," is related to tamim, "wholehearted" (15:2).

a: you test hearts and kidneys
p: In Hebrew the heart thinks and the kidneys feel. God tests both: the whole inner life.
b: Libbot u-khelayot, "hearts and kidneys," was "hearts and reins" in the KJV (Latin renes, kidneys). For Israel the heart was the seat of thought and will, the kidneys of the deepest feelings and conscience (16:7; Jeremiah 12:2). Jeremiah uses the same pair of God who "tests heart and kidneys" (Jeremiah 11:20; Jeremiah 17:10), and Revelation 2:23 echoes it. English would say "mind and heart."

a: If one does not turn back
p: The verse does not say. It may be God, ready to judge, or the wicked man, ready to attack.
b: The Hebrew has only "he." Most versions supply "God": if a man does not repent, God will sharpen his sword. But some scholars, noting 7:14–16, read the wicked man as the subject: if he does not turn, he keeps sharpening his sword and readying his flaming arrows, only to fall into his own pit. The ambiguity may be deliberate: the violence the wicked prepares turns into God's judgment on him. "Turn back" (yashuv) is the Bible's word for repentance.

a: he goes into labor with wrong
p: Evil is pictured as a pregnancy that ends in a stillborn lie.
b: The three verbs follow a pregnancy backward and forward: he is in labor with wrong, he conceives trouble, he gives birth to a lie, that is, to nothing real, a deception that fails. Job 15:35 and Isaiah 59:4 use the same picture, and James 1:15 reworks it: "desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin... gives birth to death."

a: into the ditch he made he has fallen
p: A favorite rule of biblical wisdom: the harm you plan comes back on you.
b: The same picture appears in 9:15, 35:7–8, 57:6, Proverbs 26:27 and Ecclesiastes 10:8. The Bible does not present it as a law of nature but as God's way of ruling the world: the trap turns on the trapper. Haman, hanged on the pole he had set up for Mordecai (Esther 7:10), is the classic story of it.
r: Psalm 9:15; Psalm 35:7–8; Psalm 57:6; Proverbs 26:27; Ecclesiastes 10:8; Esther 7:10

a: the LORD Most High
p: Elyon, 'Most High', is an ancient title of God, first used by Melchizedek of Salem.
b: Elyon is the title used by Melchizedek, priest of "God Most High" in Salem (Genesis 14:18–22), and in poems that picture God over all the nations and their gods (Deuteronomy 32:8; Psalm 82:6). It returns in 9:2. The psalm ends where it began, with a turn to praise; this pattern of lament ending in thanks is typical of Book I.

a: On the gittith
p: Perhaps a lyre from Gath, or a vintage tune. The Greek read 'for the winepresses'.
b: Gittit (also 81:0 and 84:0) may come from Gath, the Philistine city where David once lived (1 Samuel 27:2–7), so "a Gittite lyre" or tune; or from gat, "winepress." The Greek and Latin read "for the winepresses" (hyper ton lenon), and so some church fathers linked the psalm with the autumn grape harvest and the Festival of Booths, while others read the winepresses as the churches. Its meaning is uncertain.

a: LORD, our Lord
p: YHWH, God's name, then Adonenu, 'our Lord', a title of a master or king.
b: The opening joins God's personal name with adonenu, "our master, our Lord," the title for a king or owner. It is the only psalm addressed wholly to God in the second person from first line to last, and it begins and ends with the same refrain (8:1, 8:9), so the human glory in the middle is framed by God's.

a: You have placed your splendor over the heavens.
p: The Hebrew 'asher tenah' looks like 'you who set!' (a command). Scholars have proposed many fixes.
b: As written, asher tenah hodekha reads "which, set your splendor," with tenah an imperative. Proposals include reading natattah, "you have set" (so most versions and the Plain); tunnah, "is sung" ("whose splendor is sung above the heavens"); or linking the line with 8:2. The Greek has "for your majesty is raised above the heavens." The sense is clear even if the grammar is not: God's glory is higher than the sky.
orig: אֲשֶׁר תְּנָה הוֹדְךָ עַל־הַשָּׁמָיִם (asher tenah hodekha al-ha-shamayim)

a: Out of the mouths of children and babies at the breast
p: Jesus quotes the Greek, 'you have prepared praise', when children shout 'Hosanna' in the temple (Matthew 21:16).
b: The Hebrew says God has founded 'oz, "strength" or "a stronghold," out of the mouths of children. The Greek translated 'oz as "praise" (ainon), a meaning the word can have in a few poems (29:1; 96:7). In Matthew 21:15–16, when the chief priests object to children shouting "Hosanna to the Son of David," Jesus answers with the Greek of this verse. How babies' cries defeat enemies is a puzzle: perhaps the weakest voices praising God are enough to silence the strongest opposition (compare 1 Corinthians 1:27). Some Christians draw on the verse in discussing infant faith; see the box on the chapter page.
orig: מִפִּי עוֹלְלִים וְיֹנְקִים יִסַּדְתָּ עֹז (mi-pi olelim ve-yoneqim yissadta 'oz)

a: the enemy and the one bent on revenge
p: Some scholars see an echo of the chaos powers God defeated when he made the world.
b: Why enemies in a creation hymn? Many scholars hear an echo of an old picture, shared with Israel's neighbors, in which a god made the world after defeating the forces of chaos (compare 74:13–17; 89:9–11; and the Babylonian Enuma Elish). In Psalm 8 there is no battle and no monster: God's weapon is the voice of babies, which may be a deliberate contrast with such myths. Other interpreters take the enemies simply as those who deny God, as in 14:1.

a: the work of your fingers
p: The heavens, so vast to us, are finger-work for God, delicate needlework rather than heavy labor.
b: Elsewhere God makes the world by his "hand" or "arm"; here the sky is the work of his "fingers," like embroidery. The sun is not mentioned: the poet looks at the night sky. The "finger of God" also writes the tablets of the law (Exodus 31:18) and, in Jesus' words, drives out demons (Luke 11:20).

a: what is a mere mortal, that you remember him
p: The question is asked again, in other moods, in Psalm 144:3 and Job 7:17–18. Hebrews 2:6–8 applies it to Jesus.
b: Enosh is a human being in his weakness (103:15); ben adam, "son of man," means simply a human being, one of Adam's line (compare Ezekiel 2:1). Psalm 144:3–4 repeats the question in wonder at human frailty; Job turns it bitterly, asking why God watches a man so closely (Job 7:17–18). Hebrews 2:6–9 quotes the Greek of 8:4–6 and applies it to Jesus, who "for a little while was made lower than the angels" and now is crowned with glory: the human destiny of Psalm 8, not yet seen in all people, is seen in him. Christian readers have also heard in "son of man" an echo of Jesus' favorite title for himself, though the Gospels do not quote Psalm 8 for it.

a: You made him only a little less than God
t: Less than God, or than angels?
p: The Hebrew is elohim. It can mean God or divine beings. The Greek and Hebrews 2:7 have 'angels'.
b: Elohim usually means "God," but it can also mean heavenly beings, the members of God's court (82:1, 6). The Greek, the Targum and the Syriac, followed by the Vulgate, the KJV and Hebrews 2:7, read "angels." Many modern versions read "God" or "heavenly beings." Psalm 8 echoes Genesis 1:26–28, where humans are made in God's image and given rule over the creatures; on that reading "a little less than God" fits. The medieval Jewish commentators Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak also read "angels" here. The Plain follows the plain sense of the Hebrew word and shows the Greek as a variant.

a: everything you have placed beneath his feet
p: Paul uses this line for Christ's victory over every power, death included (1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:22).
b: Putting something "under the feet" was a picture of conquest: kings put their feet on the necks of defeated rulers (Joshua 10:24; compare Psalm 110:1). Psalm 8 gives humans a royal rule over the animals, as in Genesis 1:28. The New Testament applies the line to Christ as the true human ruler: "he has put all things in subjection under his feet" (1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:22; Hebrews 2:8), so that even death is included. Modern readers have also asked what "rule" means for the care of the earth; many Jewish and Christian teachers read it as a steward's rule, not a license to destroy.
r: Genesis 1:28; Psalm 110:1; Joshua 10:24; 1 Corinthians 15:25–27; Ephesians 1:22; Hebrews 2:8

a: the birds of the air, the fish of the sea
p: The list runs from tame animals to wild ones, then birds and fish, the creatures of Genesis 1:26–28.
b: Psalm 8:7–8 names sheep and cattle, wild animals, birds and fish: the creatures over which Genesis 1:26–28 gives humans rule, though in a different order, moving outward from the farm to the open country, the sky and the sea. Whatever "crosses the roads through the seas" probably means the sea creatures, perhaps including the great ones of 104:26. The psalm does not mention the sun or the work of the six days: it is a meditation on the human place in creation, not a retelling of it.

a: On muth-labben
p: Read as 'death of the son', 'for the young women', or a tune. Its meaning is lost.
b: Al-mut labben has been read as "on the death of the son" (Hebrew mut, die; ben, son), as a tune name, or (with the Greek, "for the secret things of the son") as alamot, "young women" (a soprano register, compare 46:0 and 1 Chronicles 15:20). The Targum reads "on the death of the man who went out between the camps," that is, Goliath (1 Samuel 17:4, where the Hebrew calls him "the man of the in-between"), and Rashi records the same tradition.

a: With all my heart I will thank the LORD
p: Psalms 9 and 10 form one alphabet poem. The Greek and Latin count them as one psalm.
b: Psalms 9 and 10 are an acrostic: in the Hebrew, most pairs of verses begin with the next letter of the alphabet. Psalm 9 runs from alef (9:1) through about kaf (9:18), and Psalm 10 begins with lamed (10:1) and ends with qof, resh, shin and tav (10:12–17). Several letters are missing in the middle of Psalm 10. Psalm 10 has no title, unusual in Book I, and Selah ends 9:20, as if a pause came there. The Old Greek and the Vulgate count 9 and 10 as one psalm (Psalm 9), so from here to Psalm 147 their numbers are usually one lower than the Hebrew and English. Many scholars think one poem was later split in two for worship; others think two related poems were joined.

a: you sat down on the throne, judging fairly
p: An ancient king judged from his throne. God sits as judge over the nations.
b: In Israel, as in its neighbors, the king's throne was also the highest court (1 Kings 3:16–28; 1 Kings 7:7). Psalms 9–10 picture the LORD seated as judge of the world, taking up the case of the poor against the nations and the wicked (9:7–8). The picture is grand in scale but its concern is the helpless (9:9; 10:14).

a: a high tower for the downtrodden
t: A high place out of reach
p: Misgav is a fort on a height, too high for an enemy to reach.
b: Misgav comes from a verb meaning "to be high, out of reach." A misgav was a refuge on high ground (18:2; 46:7). The dakh, "downtrodden, crushed," are those beaten down by others. The God who sits on the throne of 9:7 is a fortress for the lowest.

a: the one who avenges blood
p: God takes the part of the murdered and demands an account, as a family avenger did.
b: Doresh damim, "seeker of blood," is the one who demands an account for bloodshed, as God does in Genesis 9:5 ("for your own blood, your lives, I will demand a reckoning"). In Israel a relative, the "avenger of blood," had that duty (Numbers 35:19); here God himself takes it for the poor who have no one. "Remembered them" means the slain or the afflicted: God has not forgotten what was done to them.

a: the gates of death
t: The gates of death and of Zion
p: Death is pictured as a city with gates. God lifts the psalmist from its gates to the gates of Zion.
b: Sheol was pictured as a walled city or prison with gates (107:18; Isaiah 38:10; Job 38:17). The psalmist, close to death, asks to be lifted out of its gates so that he may praise God in the gates of "Daughter Zion," a poetic name for Jerusalem's people (9:14). Jesus' words "the gates of Hades will not be stronger than it" (Matthew 16:18) use the same picture.

a: Higgaion. Selah
p: From hagah, 'murmur'. Perhaps a soft musical interlude, or a call to reflect.
b: Higgayon is from the same root as hagah in 1:2. In 92:3 it seems to mean the sound of the lyre, and in 19:14 the "meditation" of the heart. Here, joined with Selah, it is probably a musical or liturgical direction, perhaps a quiet interlude.

a: The wicked will go back to Sheol
p: The world of the dead, under the earth, where all go. It is not the same as 'hell' in later Christian teaching.
b: She'ol is the Hebrew name for the place of the dead, pictured under the earth, dark and silent (6:5; 88:3–6). The KJV often translates it "hell" (as here) or "the grave." In most of the Old Testament, good and bad alike go to Sheol; it is not a place of punishment, though going there early, cut off in judgment, is the fate of the wicked here. "Go back" may mean they return to the dust they came from (Genesis 3:19; 90:3). Later Jewish and Christian writings developed ideas of reward and punishment after death, and the Greek translators used hades.

a: Let the nations learn that they are mere mortals.
p: Psalms 9–10 mix two enemies: foreign nations and wicked people inside Israel.
b: Psalm 9 speaks mostly of "the nations" (9:5, 15, 17, 19–20); Psalm 10 mostly of "the wicked" man who preys on the poor at home (10:2–11). The poem joins them: arrogance against God and cruelty to the weak are the same sin, wherever it is found. The last line is a prayer that the proud would learn their limits: enosh, "mortal," is the weak human being of 8:4.

a: LORD, why keep standing at a distance?
p: Psalm 10 opens with the 'why' of lament, the lamed line of the alphabet poem.
b: Lamah, "why," begins the lamed stanza of the acrostic (see 9:1). After the confident praise of Psalm 9, the poem now asks why God seems absent while the wicked hunt the poor. The pairing of trust and complaint in one poem is typical of the Psalms: faith speaks both ways. The words "in times of trouble" repeat 9:9 exactly, as if to ask where the "high tower in times of distress" has gone.
orig: לָמָה יְהוָה תַּעֲמֹד בְּרָחוֹק (lamah YHWH ta'amod be-rachoq)

a: he curses and spurns the LORD
p: The Hebrew says 'blesses'. It is probably a polite cover for 'curses', as in Job 1:5.
b: The verb is berekh, "blesses." Scribes sometimes wrote "bless" for "curse" when God was the object, to avoid writing a curse on God (Job 1:5; 1 Kings 21:13). So most read "the greedy man curses and spurns the LORD." Others read "the greedy man blesses himself" (congratulates himself) or "he blesses the greedy." The Greek has "the unjust man blesses himself."
orig: וּבֹצֵעַ בֵּרֵךְ נִאֵץ יְהוָה (u-votsea' berekh ni'ets YHWH)

a: "There is no God" sums up all his plans.
p: He does not deny that God exists in theory. He lives as if God will never act.
b: "There is no God" (ein Elohim) here and in 14:1 is not a philosophical denial of God. The wicked man believes God "forgets" and "never looks" (10:11) and "will not look into it" (10:13): God, if he exists, does not matter. Interpreters often call this practical atheism. The poem answers it with "You have seen it, yes, you!" (10:14).

a: Cursing fills his mouth, with tricks and abuse
p: Paul quotes this verse in the Greek: 'whose mouth is full of curses and bitterness'.
b: Romans 3:14 takes up this line in its catalogue of human sin, alongside 5:9 and 14:1–3. In the acrostic this should be the pe line, but the Hebrew begins with alah, "cursing," and pihu, "his mouth," comes second; the Greek, and Romans 3:14 after it, put "mouth" first, which may keep the older order. "Under his tongue" pictures evil kept in the mouth like a sweet one savors (Job 20:12).

a: the helpless fall into his powerful claws
p: 10:10 is one of the hardest verses in the Psalms. Both the written text and the reading tradition differ.
b: The Hebrew written text (Ketiv) and the Masoretes' reading (Qere) differ twice: "and he is crushed" or "he crushes, crouches"; and chel'ka'im, "the unfortunate" (one word, as in 10:8, 14), or chel ka'im, "an army of the dejected." The "strong ones" ('atsumav) may be the lion's claws or the wicked man's henchmen. The Plain gives the most likely sense of the lion picture of 10:9; no translation of this verse is certain. Several letters of the acrostic are missing around here, which suggests the text was damaged.
orig: יִדְכֶּה יָשֹׁחַ וְנָפַל בַּעֲצוּמָיו חֵלְכָּאִים (yidkeh yashoach ve-nafal ba'atsumav chel'ka'im)

a: You have been the orphan's helper.
p: In Israel's law and the laws of its neighbors, the king's duty was to protect orphans and widows.
b: The yatom, a child without a father, had no one to speak for him in court. Israel's law commands care for orphans, widows and foreigners (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 10:18), and the prophets condemn their neglect (Isaiah 1:17). Kings of Babylon and Ugarit also claimed to protect the orphan and widow, as Hammurabi does in the epilogue to his laws. Psalm 10 says the LORD is the true king who does this (10:16–18).
r: Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17; Psalm 68:5; Psalm 146:9; James 1:27

a: The LORD is king always and forever.
t: The answer to the absent God
p: The poem turns on the kingship of the LORD: the nations perish from his land.
b: The confession that the LORD is king anchors both halves of the poem (9:7; 10:16). "Nations have perished from his land" may look back to the conquest, or forward in hope, or may be the perfect of confidence (see 3:7). Some scholars think Psalms 9–10 were composed for the king or the community after a victory; others read them as a poor person's prayer set in the frame of God's world rule.

a: Fly off to your mountain, bird!
p: Friends tell the psalmist to escape to the hills. The Hebrew text is unsettled.
b: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has a plural, "flee (you people)!," while the reading tradition (Qere) has a feminine singular, addressed to "my soul": "flee to your mountain, bird." "Your mountain" is plural ("your [people's] mountain"). The Greek reads "Move to the mountains like a sparrow." Whatever the exact form, the friends' advice is to run, as David once ran to the hills from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14; 1 Samuel 26:20, where he calls himself a partridge hunted in the mountains). The psalmist refuses: he has already found his shelter in the LORD.

a: When the foundations are smashed
p: Who speaks this, and what are the foundations? Social order, the law, or the earth itself?
b: Most read 11:2–3 as the friends' words, continuing 11:1: the wicked are shooting in the dark, and if the very pillars of society, law and justice, are being pulled down, what can a good man do but flee? "Foundations" (shatot) is rare; the Targum and some rabbis took it as the leaders or the teachers of the law. The Hebrew "what has the righteous one done?" has been read by some interpreters of God ("what has the Righteous One done?"), but most read it of the human righteous. Psalm 11 answers in 11:4: the true foundation is the LORD on his throne.
orig: כִּי הַשָּׁתוֹת יֵהָרֵסוּן צַדִּיק מַה־פָּעָל (ki ha-shatot yeharesun tsaddiq mah-pa'al)

a: In his holy temple is the LORD
p: The LORD is in his temple and on his throne in heaven: the earthly house reflects the heavenly one.
b: The two lines set the temple (hekhal) beside the heavens. Israel thought of the Jerusalem temple as the earthly footstool of God's heavenly throne (99:5; 132:7; 1 Kings 8:27–30), and Habakkuk 2:20 uses the same words, "The LORD is in his holy temple," before a call to silence. His "eyelids" test humans: a picture of narrowed eyes, looking closely.

a: On the wicked he will rain down traps
p: The Hebrew says 'traps'. A small change gives 'coals of fire', which fits the fire-and-sulfur picture.
b: Pachim means "snares, traps." Raining traps is an odd image, so many scholars change one letter to read pachame, "coals of" (as Symmachus, a Greek translator of about AD 200, seems to have done), giving "coals of fire and sulfur." The Old Greek and the Vulgate support "snares." The "fire and sulfur" recall Sodom (Genesis 19:24), and "the portion of their cup" is the cup of judgment God gives to drink (75:8; Jeremiah 25:15).

a: those who are upright will look upon his face
p: The Hebrew can read 'the upright will see his face' or 'his face sees the upright'.
b: Yashar yechezu fanemo has a plural verb and an unusual suffix. Most modern versions read "the upright will see his face": to see God's face is to be welcomed in his presence, as at the temple (17:15; 27:4). The KJV, following the Greek and Latin, reads "his countenance doth behold the upright." Christian tradition linked the first reading with the hope of seeing God (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2).

a: the loyal one has come to an end
p: The chasid, the person of hesed, has vanished. Compare Micah 7:2.
b: Chasid, the one who shows hesed (5:7), is the loyal, faithful person. The complaint that such people have disappeared is the same as Micah 7:2 ("the loyal have vanished from the land") and Isaiah 57:1. It is the exaggeration of grief: the psalmist feels alone among liars.

a: with a divided heart
p: Hebrew 'with a heart and a heart' means two-faced: saying one thing, meaning another.
b: Be-lev va-lev is literally "with a heart and a heart": the liar has two hearts, one for show and one for real. Compare 1 Chronicles 12:33, where soldiers are praised for having "no heart and heart," and James 1:8 on the "double-minded."

a: so now I will get up," says the LORD
p: Suddenly God speaks. Many think a prophet or priest gave this answer in the temple.
b: Psalm 12 is one of the few psalms in which God answers in the first person in the middle of a lament (compare 60:6–8; 75:2–5; 91:14–16). Mowinckel and many after him think temple prophets gave such answers during worship. The last line is unclear: yafiach lo may mean "the one who pants for it" (safety), or "the one they sneer at" (KJV "from him that puffeth at him"; compare 10:5).
orig: עַתָּה אָקוּם יֹאמַר יְהוָה (attah aqum yomar YHWH)

a: silver smelted in a crucible in the ground
p: Silver ore was melted again and again in clay crucibles to remove impurities.
b: Ancient silver was refined by cupellation: the ore was melted with lead in a clay crucible, and the impurities were burned off or absorbed. "In the ground" (la-arets) is uncertain: it may mean a furnace built into the earth, or "refined (and flowing) to the ground," or it may belong with the next word. "Seven times" means completely. Against the slippery talk of people (12:2–4), the LORD's word is pure. The verse was beloved of later readers, Jewish and Christian, who applied it to the reliability of Scripture.
orig: כֶּסֶף צָרוּף בַּעֲלִיל לָאָרֶץ (kesef tsaruf ba'alil la-arets)

a: when worthlessness is raised high among people
p: The psalm ends not with praise but with the wicked still strutting about.
b: Unlike most laments, Psalm 12 does not close in thanksgiving. God's promise (12:5) and the purity of his words (12:6–7) stand in the center, but the last verse returns to the present: the wicked are everywhere while worthlessness is honored. The hope is real, but not yet seen.

a: LORD, how long will you forget me? Forever?
p: Psalm 13 is the textbook lament: complaint (13:1–2), plea (13:3–4), trust and praise (13:5–6).
b: Scholars since Gunkel use Psalm 13 to show the usual parts of an individual lament: a cry to God with a complaint, four times "how long?" (13:1–2), a request with reasons (13:3–4), and a turn to trust and a vow of praise (13:5–6). The complaint goes three ways: against God ("you forget, you hide your face"), about the self ("grief in my heart") and about the enemy ("raised above me"). "Forget" and "hide your face" are covenant words: they mean God seems to have stopped caring for his own (10:11; 44:24). Westermann and Brueggemann point out how freely Israel's faith allowed protest against God, inside prayer.

a: keep turning plans over in my mind
p: He keeps making plans, schemes for escape, that come to nothing. Some read 'pains' for 'plans'.
b: Etsot means "counsels, plans": he keeps deliberating, round and round, with no way out. Some scholars change one letter to read atsabot, "pains," to match "grief in my heart." "Day by day" (yomam) may mean "all day long."

a: Brighten my eyes, or I will fall asleep in death
p: Dull eyes are a sign of weakness and coming death. Bright eyes are life restored.
b: When Jonathan ate honey, "his eyes lit up" (1 Samuel 14:27, 29); when strength fails, the light of the eyes goes out (38:10). The psalmist asks God to restore his life before the sleep of death. The Bible often calls death "sleep" (Job 14:12; Daniel 12:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:13), and Christians took up the picture with the hope of waking (compare 17:15).

a: it is in your loyal love that I trust
p: How does lament become trust? The psalm does not explain. It simply turns.
b: Between 13:4 and 13:5 nothing in the situation has changed: the enemy is still there. The turn is an act of trust in God's hesed (see 5:7). Some scholars think a word of assurance was given at this point (see 6:8); others see a change that happens in the act of praying itself. Calvin, on this verse, sees David rising by faith above what he can see. The last line, "he has been generous to me" (gamal alai), may look back at past mercies or forward in confidence.

a: the fool says to himself
p: A naval is not stupid but morally foolish: a person who acts as if God does not matter.
b: Hebrew has several words for "fool." Naval is the worst: a person who is godless, boorish and selfish, like Nabal, the man whose name it is (1 Samuel 25:25, "Nabal is his name, and shameful folly is his companion"), or Shechem, who "had done a disgraceful thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). The fool's "There is no God" is a way of life, not a theory (see 10:4). Anselm's famous proof of God's existence (1078) begins from this verse, the "fool" who says in his heart there is no God; Anselm used the verse for a philosophical purpose the psalm does not have.

a: From heaven the LORD leans out and looks
p: The same psalm appears twice in the Psalter. Psalm 14 has 'the LORD'; Psalm 53 has 'God'.
b: Psalms 14 and 53 are the same psalm with small differences. Psalm 14 (in Book I) uses YHWH, "the LORD," four times (14:2, 14:4, 14:6, 14:7). Psalm 53 (in Book II, in the "Elohistic Psalter," 42–83) has Elohim, "God," in 53:2, 53:4 and 53:6, where 14 has 14:2, 14:4 and 14:7; the fourth (14:6) falls in the verse that 53 rewrites. The biggest difference is in 14:5–6 and 53:5 (see 14:5). Most scholars think the two versions were kept in two older collections before the Psalter was put together, and that an editor of Psalms 42–83 changed YHWH to Elohim throughout. The picture of God looking down from heaven recalls Babel and Sodom (Genesis 11:5; Genesis 18:21): God examines before he judges.

a: No one does good, no, not a single one.
p: Romans 3:10–12 quotes 14:1–3 to show all humans are under sin. The psalm itself speaks of 'the fools'.
b: Paul begins his chain of quotations in Romans 3:10–12 with this psalm: "There is no one righteous, not even one; there is no one who understands, no one who seeks God; all have turned away." In the psalm the "all" are the fools who devour "my people" (14:4), and the righteous are a separate group (14:5). Paul widens it: Israel's Scripture includes every person, Jew and Gentile, under sin, so that grace is the only way (Romans 3:19–24). Many Christian traditions read the verse as a statement of universal sinfulness; Jewish interpreters read it of the wicked of a given generation (Rashi says David foresaw Nebuchadnezzar's armies destroying the temple).

a: They devour my people as they would eat bread
p: 'My people' is God's voice, or the prophet's. The oppressors live off the poor like a daily meal.
b: The speaker suddenly says "my people," probably God himself, as in the prophets (Micah 3:3, "who eat the flesh of my people"). The oppressors devour the poor as casually as eating bread, and "do not call on the LORD," because they think he will not act. Some scholars see here the language of temple prophets condemning the powerful in Jerusalem.

a: There they shook with dread
p: Here the two versions differ most. Psalm 53:5 speaks of God scattering the bones of the besieger.
b: Psalm 14:5–6 speaks of terror falling on the oppressors because God is with the righteous, and of their shaming the poor man's plans. The parallel in 53:5 begins the same way and then goes on differently: "There they shook with dread, / where no dread had been. / For God has scattered the bones of your besieger. / You have put them to shame, because God has thrown them away." Some scholars think 53 was reshaped after a military rescue, perhaps the Assyrian siege of 701 BC (2 Kings 19:35); others think 14 is the reworked version, or that both grew from a damaged text. "There" may be a place (Zion, the battlefield) or "then."

a: When the LORD brings his people back from captivity
p: Shuv shevut can mean 'bring back the captives' or 'restore the fortunes'. Many think 14:7 was added in the exile.
b: Shuv shevut is a set phrase. Older versions read "bring back the captivity" (KJV), linking shevut with shevi, "captivity." Many modern scholars take it as "restore the fortunes," a reversal of disaster in general (Job 42:10, where Job was never a captive). Because it fits the return from Babylon so well (126:1, 4), many think 14:7 was added to the psalm in or after the exile to make it the prayer of the whole people. "Who will send...?" (mi yitten) is the Hebrew way of saying "If only!"
orig: בְּשׁוּב יְהוָה שְׁבוּת עַמּוֹ (be-shuv YHWH shevut ammo)

a: LORD, who is welcome as a guest in your tent?
p: Worshipers at the temple gate ask who may enter. A priest answers with a list of right actions.
b: Psalm 15 and Psalm 24:3–6 are often called "entrance liturgies" or "torah liturgies": pilgrims arriving at the sanctuary ask who may enter, and the gatekeeper or priest answers (compare Isaiah 33:14–16). "Tent" recalls the tent David pitched for the ark on Zion (2 Samuel 6:17) and the desert tabernacle; "stay as a guest" (yagur) uses the word for a resident foreigner under protection (see 5:4). The answer is ethical, not ritual: it says nothing about sacrifices or cleanness, only about how one lives and speaks.

a: One who walks with a whole heart
p: Tamim is 'complete, whole': not sinless, but undivided in loyalty.
b: Tamim is used of sacrificial animals without defect and of people whose loyalty to God is whole, like Noah (Genesis 6:9) and Abraham (Genesis 17:1). For people the shared terms give "wholehearted"; here the Plain says "walks with a whole heart," the same sense in a form that reads more easily. "Speaks the truth inside his heart" means he is honest even in his own thoughts, the opposite of the "divided heart" of 12:2.

a: His tongue does not go around spreading gossip.
p: Ragal, from regel 'foot', means to go about as a talebearer.
b: The verb ragal comes from the word for foot: the slanderer goes from house to house carrying stories (compare Leviticus 19:16, "Do not go about as a slanderer among your kin"). Three of the psalm's ten or so marks of the righteous concern speech: truth in the heart, no gossip, no insult (15:2–3).

a: A rejected man is worthless in his eyes
p: The rabbis read the line of humility: he is lowly in his own eyes.
b: The Hebrew nivzeh be-'enav nim'as can be read "despised in his eyes is the reprobate" (most versions): the righteous does not flatter powerful wrongdoers but honors the God-fearing, however poor. The Talmud (Makkot 24a) reads it of King Hezekiah, who dragged his wicked father's bones on a rope bed, and others read it of humility: "he is despised and lowly in his own eyes." The same passage of the Talmud says David "reduced" the 613 commandments of the Torah to the eleven of Psalm 15.

a: He swears to his own cost and does not go back on it.
p: He keeps his word even when keeping it hurts him. The Greek reads 'swears to his neighbor'.
b: Nishba' le-hara' means "he swears to do harm" or "to his harm": having made a promise, he keeps it even when it costs him (compare Joshua 9:19–20, Jephthah in Judges 11:35). The Greek read the consonants as le-rea', "to his neighbor": "who swears to his neighbor and does not break it." The Hebrew is followed here.
orig: נִשְׁבַּע לְהָרַע וְלֹא יָמִר (nishba' le-hara' ve-lo yamir)

a: He lends his silver without charging interest
p: Israel's law forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite in need.
b: Loans in ancient Israel were mostly to the poor in hard times, not business investments. The law forbids charging neshekh, interest (literally "a bite"), on such loans to fellow Israelites (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 23:19–20). Ancient Near Eastern interest rates could reach 20 to 33 percent a year on silver and more on grain. Christians long applied this to all lending; the medieval church forbade usury, and Calvin and others later argued that moderate interest on business loans was not what the law forbade. "Takes no payment to harm the innocent" forbids bribing a judge or witness (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19).

a: A miktam of David
p: Six psalms are called miktam (16, 56–60). The word is unexplained; the Greek has 'inscription on a stone'.
b: Miktam heads Psalm 16 and 56–60. Proposals include "inscription" (so the Greek stelographia, "writing on a pillar," and the Targum, "an upright engraving"), "golden" poem (from ketem, gold, so "a golden psalm" in older English), and "atonement" or "secret" psalm. All are guesses.

a: Nothing good is mine beyond you.
p: Tovati bal-'alekha: 'my good is not beyond you'. The Greek has 'you have no need of my goods'.
b: The words tovati bal-'alekha are short and difficult. Most read "I have no good apart from you": God is the psalmist's only good. The KJV read "my goodness extendeth not to thee," and the Greek "you have no need of my good things," both taking it to mean God gains nothing from human goodness (compare Job 22:2–3). The Plain gives the reading that best fits 16:5–6, where the LORD himself is the psalmist's share.

a: As for the holy ones who are in the land
p: The 'holy ones' may be God's faithful people, or the gods of the land, which the psalmist renounces.
b: The verse is perhaps the hardest in Book I. Older Jewish and Christian readers took the "holy ones" as faithful Israelites, "the saints in the land," in whom the psalmist delights. Many modern scholars read 16:3–4 together as a renunciation of other gods: "holy ones" and "mighty ones" (addirim) were titles of the gods of Canaan, and 16:4 speaks of their worshipers, their drink offerings and their names. On that reading, the psalmist once honored them, or is tempted to, and now refuses. The Greek reads: "For the holy ones in his land, he made wonderful all his will in them." The Plain keeps the Hebrew's ambiguity.
orig: לִקְדוֹשִׁים אֲשֶׁר־בָּאָרֶץ הֵמָּה וְאַדִּירֵי (li-qdoshim asher ba-arets hemmah ve'addire)

a: I will not pour drink offerings of blood to them
p: Libations of wine were poured to gods. 'Of blood' may mean offerings by violent men, or rites the law forbade.
b: A drink offering (nesekh) was wine or water poured on an altar; Israel offered them to the LORD (Numbers 15:5–10). "Drink offerings of blood" may be literal blood rites of other cults, forbidden in Israel (Leviticus 17:10–12), or offerings stained by bloodshed (Isaiah 66:3). Not taking the names of other gods on one's lips echoes Exodus 23:13 and Joshua 23:7.

a: The LORD is the share I was given, and my cup.
p: When the land was divided, the Levites got no territory: 'I am your share' (Numbers 18:20).
b: The language of 16:5–6 is the language of land division by lot: share (cheleq), lot (goral), measuring lines (chavalim), inheritance (nachalah). Every tribe received land, except Levi, to whom the LORD said, "I am your portion and your inheritance" (Numbers 18:20; compare Deuteronomy 10:9). Some scholars therefore think Psalm 16 was a Levite's or priest's prayer. In Israel and in the church it became the prayer of anyone whose real wealth is God himself. The "cup" is one's lot in life (11:6; 23:5).
r: Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9; Joshua 18:6–10; Psalm 73:26; Lamentations 3:24; Psalm 23:5

a: I have placed the LORD in front of me at all times
p: Acts 2:25–28 quotes 16:8–11 in the Greek as David speaking of Christ's resurrection.
b: In his sermon at Pentecost Peter quotes 16:8–11 (Greek) and argues: David died and was buried, and his tomb is still here; so he was speaking as a prophet about the resurrection of the Messiah, whose flesh did not see decay (Acts 2:25–32). Paul makes the same argument from 16:10 in Acts 13:35–37. Jewish interpreters read the psalm of David himself, confident that God would protect him from early death (Rashi), or of the soul's survival (Radak, Ibn Ezra on 16:10–11). The Hebrew shivviti ("I have placed") opens a famous Jewish devotional plaque, the shiviti, hung in synagogues facing the prayer leader with the words of 16:8.
orig: שִׁוִּיתִי יְהוָה לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד (shivviti YHWH le-negdi tamid)

a: my honor celebrates
p: Kevodi, 'my honor', may mean 'my whole self' or even 'my liver'. The Greek, quoted in Acts 2:26, has 'my tongue'.
b: Kevodi is "my glory, my honor." In poetry it often stands for one's whole self (7:5; 30:12; 57:8); some scholars repoint it kevedi, "my liver," the seat of feeling, matching "heart" and "flesh." The Greek translators wrote "my tongue," and Acts 2:26 quotes that. The Greek of the next line, "my flesh will dwell in hope," also differs from the Hebrew "in safety" (la-vetach).

a: you will not allow your loyal one to see the Pit
p: Shachat means 'pit', the grave. The Greek translated it 'corruption, decay', and Acts builds on that.
b: Shachat usually means "pit," a name for the grave or Sheol (30:9; Job 33:18), parallel to Sheol in the first line. The Greek translated it diaphthora, "corruption, decay," possibly linking it with the verb shachat, "to ruin, spoil." Peter and Paul argue from the Greek wording: David's body decayed, so "your holy one will not see decay" must speak of Jesus (Acts 2:27, 31; Acts 13:35–37). In the Hebrew the psalmist expects God to keep him from death, either now (rescued from early death) or, as many Jewish and Christian readers came to hold, beyond it. On "your loyal one" and its plural spelling in many manuscripts, see the variant. On Christ's descent and this verse, see the box on the chapter page.
orig: לֹא־תִתֵּן חֲסִידְךָ לִרְאוֹת שָׁחַת (lo-titten chasidkha lir'ot shachat)
r: Acts 2:27; Acts 2:31; Acts 13:35–37; Psalm 30:9; Psalm 49:15; Job 33:18

a: You let me know the path of life.
p: Does the psalm hope for life after death? Scholars disagree; the New Testament says yes.
b: "The path of life" in Proverbs means a good life now (Proverbs 15:24). "Delights that never end" (netsach, "forever, to the end") and the contrast with Sheol and the Pit (16:10) push toward more. Many critical scholars (Kraus, for example) read the psalm as trust for rescue in this life; others (Dahood, and many Christian scholars, and Jewish commentators from the Middle Ages on) see a hope of unending life with God, like 49:15 and 73:23–26. The New Testament reads it as fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 2:28).

a: A prayer of David
p: Tefillah, 'a prayer', heads five psalms (17, 86, 90, 102, 142). The colophon at 72:20 calls all David's psalms 'prayers'.
b: Tefillah is the ordinary word for prayer. It heads Psalms 17, 86, 90, 102 and 142, and 72:20 closes Book II with "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse." Psalm 17 is a prayer of an innocent person under attack, perhaps one who spent the night in the temple awaiting God's verdict (17:3, 15).

a: You have put me through the fire, and you find nothing.
p: Like 7:3–5 and 26, the psalmist protests his innocence. Readers have weighed this against confession psalms.
b: Psalms 7, 17 and 26 make strong claims of innocence: God has tested and refined (tsaraf, the word of 12:6) and found nothing. Some scholars see the prayer of an accused person after a night in the temple, a kind of trial by ordeal (compare 1 Kings 8:31–32). Christian readers have asked how this fits with 14:3 ("no one does good") and 143:2. Augustine read it as the voice of Christ, the only truly innocent one; Calvin as a clear conscience in a particular case, not a claim to be sinless. The end of the verse is difficult (zammoti bal-ya'avor-pi): perhaps "my thoughts do not go beyond my mouth," that is, he says what he means.

a: Make your acts of loyal love wonderful
p: 'Make wonderful', 'right hand', 'your loyal love': the language of the Song of the Sea.
b: Hafleh chasadekha, "make your loyal loves wonderful," uses the word for God's "wonders" (nifla'ot, 9:1), the great acts of the exodus. "Your right hand" saved Israel at the sea (Exodus 15:6, 12–13, where God's hesed also leads them). The psalmist asks God to do for him in his small crisis what he did for Israel.

a: Guard me like the pupil of the eye.
p: Literally 'the little man, daughter of the eye': the pupil, where you see yourself reflected.
b: Ishon bat-'ayin means "the little man, the daughter of the eye": the pupil, perhaps because you can see a tiny image of yourself in someone's eye. It is the most guarded part of the body. The same phrase describes God's care for Israel in the desert (Deuteronomy 32:10). The English "apple of the eye" comes from the old idea that the pupil was a round solid object.

a: Hide me in the shade of your wings
p: A mother bird's wings, or the cherubim's wings over the ark? Both have been seen here.
b: The picture is a bird sheltering its young (Deuteronomy 32:11; Matthew 23:37). Some scholars think the phrase also recalls the wings of the cherubim spread over the ark in the temple's inner room (1 Kings 6:23–28), so that to shelter under God's wings is to shelter in his house (36:7; 61:4). Boaz blesses Ruth as one "under whose wings you have come for refuge" (Ruth 2:12).
r: Deuteronomy 32:11; Ruth 2:12; Psalm 36:7; Psalm 57:1; Psalm 61:4; Psalm 91:4; Matthew 23:37; 1 Kings 6:23–28

a: They have closed up their fat
p: Fat around the heart pictures insensitivity: a heart so padded it cannot feel.
b: Chelbamo sageru, "they have closed their fat," pictures a heart enclosed in fat, deaf to pity (73:7; 119:70; compare Isaiah 6:10, "make the heart of this people fat"). The KJV took it as "they are inclosed in their own fat." Some scholars repoint to read "the fat of their heart they have shut."

a: You fill their belly with what you have stored up
p: Is God filling the wicked with punishment, or his treasured people with good? The Hebrew allows both.
b: 17:14 is very hard. One reading (most modern versions, the Plain): the wicked are "men of this world" whose only share is in this life; God fills them with what he has stored up, either the riches they love (so they and their children are satisfied, but that is all they get), or the punishment stored up for them, to be passed on to their children. Another reading takes the second half of the verse of God's people: "your treasured ones" (following the Qere tsefunekha) you fill, their sons are satisfied. The first half is also uncertain: "from men, by your hand" may be read "slay them with your hand." The verse sets the wicked's satisfaction with things (17:14) against the psalmist's satisfaction with God (17:15).

a: When I wake up, I will be filled with the sight of your form.
p: Waking after a night in the temple, or waking from death? The Greek has 'when your glory appears'.
b: "Your form" (temunah) is what Moses saw (Numbers 12:8), and what Israel did not see at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:12). Some scholars read the verse of a worshiper who spent the night in the sanctuary and in the morning receives God's favorable verdict, "seeing his face" (compare 11:7; 27:4). Many Jewish and Christian readers, from the church fathers to modern scholars like Dahood, hear a hope beyond death: waking from the sleep of death (13:3; Daniel 12:2) to see God. The Greek has "I will be satisfied when your glory appears," with no "waking."
r: Numbers 12:8; Deuteronomy 4:12; Psalm 11:7; Psalm 13:3; Daniel 12:2; 1 John 3:2
